facts.fact_text: On 17 August 2010 the applicant notified the Lviv City Mayor on behalf of a local human-rights NGO called 'Vartovi zakonu' of its intention to hold a demonstration every Tuesday from 10.30 a.m. to 1 p.m. near the building of the Lviv Regional Prosecutor's Office.
On Tuesday 12 October 2010, further to his previous announcement of 17 August 2010, the applicant informed the Lviv City Council about the demonstration to be held on that particular day.
On 12 October 2010 the applicant organised a peaceful demonstration near the Lviv Regional Prosecutor's Office between 11.30 a.m. and 12.40 p.m.
About twenty-five persons took part in the demonstration on 12 October 2010 near the Lviv Regional Prosecutor's Office.

During the demonstration on 12 October 2010, the demonstrators were standing on the pavement in front of the building of the Lviv Regional Prosecutor's Office when the police told them that they should remain at a distance of five metres from the building.

The police told the demonstrators that they could not stand on the lawn and should move away, which would have meant standing in the road again and obstructing the traffic, causing temporary traffic-jams.
The two police officers grabbed the applicant's arms and took him in the direction of the nearby police station.

On 13 October 2010 the Lviv Regional Administrative Court granted a request by the Executive Committee of the Lviv City Council to prohibit the holding of the pre-announced demonstrations by the applicant's NGO 'Vartovi zakonu' as from 19 October 2010.

According to the applicant, upon his arrival at the Galytskyy District Police Station at about 5 p.m. on 13 October 2010, the police accused the applicant of having committed the administrative offence of malicious disobedience to a lawful order by the police on 12 October 2010.

According to the applicant, upon his arrival at the Galytskyy District Police Station at about 5 p.m. on 13 October 2010, the police accused the applicant of having committed the administrative offence of breaching the procedure for organising and holding a demonstration on 12 October 2010.
According to the applicant, at 11 p.m. on 13 October 2010 the applicant was placed in a cell at the Galytskyy District Police Station.
By a decision of 14 October 2010, the Galytskyy District Court found the applicant guilty of committing the administrative offence of malicious disobedience to a lawful order by the police.

By a decision of 14 October 2010, the Galytskyy District Court found the applicant guilty of committing the administrative offence of breaching the procedure for organising and holding a demonstration.

The Galytskyy District Court sentenced the applicant to three days of administrative detention starting from 6 p.m. on 14 October 2010, with reference to the relevant provisions of the Code on Administrative Offences.
At around 6 p.m. on 17 October 2010 the applicant was released from administrative detention.

In the reports drawn up on 14 October 2010, the police referred to provisions of the Code on Administrative Offences and to the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the city of Lviv.

In his appeal of 18 October 2010, the applicant argued that the requirement of notification two days in advance established by the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the city of Lviv, to which the police referred in their reports on administrative offences, was not based on law.

Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine provides that citizens have the right to assemble peacefully without arms and to hold meetings, rallies, marches and demonstrations, after notifying the executive authorities and bodies of local self-government beforehand.

Article 185 of the Code on Administrative Offences provides that malicious disobedience to a lawful order or demand by a police officer who is carrying out his official duties shall be punishable by a fine of between eight and fifteen times the minimum monthly wage, or by correctional labour of between one and two months with a deduction of 20% of earnings, or, in the event that in the particular circumstances of the case and with regard to the offender's character these measures are found to be insufficient, by administrative detention of up to fifteen days.

Article 185-1 of the Code on Administrative Offences provides that a breach of the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations shall be punishable by a reprimand or by a fine of between ten and twenty-five times the minimum monthly wage.

Article 185-1 of the Code on Administrative Offences provides that the same actions committed within a year of the application of administrative penalties or by the organiser of the meeting, rally, street procession or demonstration shall be punishable by a fine of between twenty and one hundred times the minimum monthly wage, or by correctional labour of one to two months with a deduction of 20% of earnings, or by administrative detention of up to fifteen days.

The Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 on the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the USSR lays down the procedure for seeking and granting permission to organise and hold meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations.

The Decision of the Executive Committee of the Lviv City Council of 16 April 2004 on the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the city of Lviv introduced the procedure for organising peaceful gatherings in the city of Lviv.

Item 7 of the procedure introduced by the Decision of the Executive Committee of the Lviv City Council of 16 April 2004 provided that notification about a planned gathering had to be given at least two working days prior to the date on which it was to be held.

Item 14 of the procedure introduced by the Decision of the Executive Committee of the Lviv City Council of 16 April 2004 specified that gatherings could not be held in the road (except street marches and demonstrations), on lawns and flower beds, or in front of the central entrance (not closer than seven metres) and other entrances of administrative buildings, nor in case of non-compliance with sanitary norms.

Item 16 of the procedure introduced by the Decision of the Executive Committee of the Lviv City Council of 16 April 2004 specified that holding a gathering in breach of any of the restrictions imposed by item 14 should be considered a breach of the peace and should engage liability under the law.

In its decision of 19 April 2001, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine held that the Ministry of the Interior of Ukraine had applied to the Constitutional Court of Ukraine for an official interpretation of the provisions of Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine regarding timely notification to executive authorities or bodies of local self-government of planned meetings, rallies, marches or demonstrations.

In its decision of 19 April 2001, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine noted that the current legislation of Ukraine did not provide for a specific time-limit within which the executive authorities or bodies of local self-government were to be notified about planned meetings, rallies, marches or demonstrations.

In its decision of 19 April 2001, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine held that the provisions of the first part of Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine on timely notification to the executive authorities or bodies of local self-government about planned meetings, rallies, marches or demonstrations shall be understood to mean that organisers must inform the authorities in advance, that is, within a reasonable time prior to the date of the planned event.

In its decision of 19 April 2001, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine held that specifying the exact deadlines for timely notification with regard to the particularities of different forms of peaceful assembly, the number of participants, the venue, and the time of the event is a matter for legislative regulation.

In its review of 1 March 2006, the Supreme Court of Ukraine noted that according to the Resolution of the Verkhovna Rada of Ukraine of 12 September 1991 No. 1545-XII on temporary application of certain legislative acts of the Soviet Union, the normative acts of the USSR remain in force, including the Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 on the procedure for organising and holding meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the USSR.

The Information note of April 2012 by the Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine on a study and summary of the jurisprudence of administrative courts applying the relevant legislation and deciding cases concerning the exercise of the right to peaceful assembly in 2010 and 2011 noted that the legislation of Ukraine does not currently have a special law regulating public relations in the sphere of peaceful assembly.

The Information note of April 2012 by the Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine noted that Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine, while providing that the executive authorities or bodies of local self-government must be notified in a timely manner that a peaceful gathering is to be held, does not establish specific deadlines for such notification, resulting in inconsistent application of the constitutional norm.

The Information note of April 2012 by the Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine noted that judicial practice contained instances of cases restricting the right to peaceful assembly being decided on the basis of the Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 No. 9306-XI on the procedure for organisation and holding of meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the USSR, and that this approach was incorrect.

The Information note of April 2012 by the Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine noted that the norms of the Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 establish the procedure for authorising (registering) peaceful assembly and empower the authorities and bodies of local self-governments to ban such events, whereas the norms of the Constitution of Ukraine provide for a procedure whereby the authorities are notified that a gathering is to be held and provide that only the courts have power to ban a peaceful gathering.

The Information note of April 2012 by the Higher Administrative Court of Ukraine concluded that the Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 should not be applied by courts when deciding cases concerning the right to peaceful assembly.

In its decision of 16 May 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that the Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 conflicted with the Constitution of Ukraine as it required the organisers to seek permission to hold a demonstration and authorised the executive authorities to ban such an event, whereas Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine provided that the authorities should be notified that a demonstration was being planned and empowered only the judicial authorities to place restrictions on the organisation thereof.

In its decision of 11 October 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that the first-instance Kyiv Administrative Court had had regard to the provisions of the Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988, whereas since 1996 the question of holding peaceful gatherings had been regulated by the Constitution of Ukraine.

In its decision of 11 October 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal stated that the Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 conflicted with the Constitution of Ukraine as it provided for a procedure for seeking permission to hold a demonstration and concerned the holding of such events in a non-existent country (the USSR), regulated relations between the citizens of the USSR and the executive committees of the Soviets of People's Deputies, and considered demonstrations on the basis of their compatibility with the Constitution of the USSR and the constitutions of the union and the autonomous republics.

In its decision of 11 October 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that under the Constitution of Ukraine human rights and freedoms, and the relevant safeguards, could be defined only by the laws of Ukraine.
The information letter of the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine of 26 November 2009 noted that the current legislation on the organisation and holding of peaceful demonstrations is not perfect.

The information letter of the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine of 26 November 2009 noted that the organisation and conduct of peaceful demonstrations is regulated by the Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 No. 9306 on the organisation and holding of meetings, rallies, street marches and demonstrations in the USSR, which is effective in so far as it does not contradict the Constitution of Ukraine pursuant to paragraph 1 of Chapter XV (Transitional Provisions) of the Constitution of Ukraine.

The information letter of the Ministry of Justice of Ukraine of 26 November 2009 noted that the requirements as to the organisation and holding of peaceful demonstrations, the time-limit for notification to be given to executive or local government bodies, and the documents to be attached to the application for holding the event are currently not regulated by law.
The Galytskyy District Court noted in its decision of 14 October 2010 that the applicant had ignored the lawful demands of the police to stop breaching the peace.

The Decree of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the USSR of 28 July 1988 provides that the executive committee of the Soviet of people's deputies shall ban a meeting, rally, street procession or demonstration if the goal of the event is contrary to the Constitution of the USSR, the Constitutions of the Republics of the Union or of the autonomous republics, or poses a threat to the public order and safety of citizens.

According to the Decision of the Executive Committee of the Lviv City Council of 16 April 2004, the freedom of assembly was guaranteed but could be restricted by a court for considerations of public health, prevention of crime and disorder, and protection of the rights of others.

Item 14 of the procedure introduced by the Decision of the Executive Committee of the Lviv City Council of 16 April 2004 specified that gatherings could not be held in the road (except street marches and demonstrations), on lawns and flower beds, or in front of the central entrance (not closer than seven metres) and other entrances of administrative buildings, nor in case of non-compliance with sanitary norms.

Item 16 of the procedure introduced by the Decision of the Executive Committee of the Lviv City Council of 16 April 2004 specified that holding a gathering in breach of any of the restrictions imposed by item 14 should be considered a breach of the peace and should engage liability under the law.

During the demonstration on 12 October 2010, the demonstrators were standing on the pavement in front of the building of the Lviv Regional Prosecutor's Office when the police told them that they should remain at a distance of five metres from the building.
The police's instruction to remain five metres from the building of the Lviv Regional Prosecutor's Office would have forced the demonstrators to stand in the road and obstruct the traffic.

After some discussion with the police during the demonstration on 12 October 2010, the demonstrators crossed the road and stood on a lawn on the opposite side of the street from the Lviv Regional Prosecutor's Office.

The police told the demonstrators that they could not stand on the lawn and should move away, which would have meant standing in the road again and obstructing the traffic, causing temporary traffic-jams.
The two police officers grabbed the applicant's arms and took him in the direction of the nearby police station.
After the demonstrators requested identification and started filming, the police officers let the applicant go.
According to the applicant, at 11 p.m. on 13 October 2010 the applicant was placed in a cell at the Galytskyy District Police Station.
According to the applicant, the applicant remained in the cell without food from 11 p.m. on 13 October 2010 until 3 p.m. on 14 October 2010.

During the hearing at the Galytskyy District Court on 14 October 2010, the court rejected the applicant's request to be represented by the lawyer of his choosing on the ground that the applicant was a human-rights defender and could defend himself.
During the hearing at the Galytskyy District Court on 14 October 2010, the court rejected the applicant's request to summon and question witnesses.
During the hearing at the Galytskyy District Court on 14 October 2010, the court rejected the applicant's request to examine a video made during the events of 12 October 2010.
By a decision of 14 October 2010, the Galytskyy District Court found the applicant guilty of committing the administrative offence of malicious disobedience to a lawful order by the police.

By a decision of 14 October 2010, the Galytskyy District Court found the applicant guilty of committing the administrative offence of breaching the procedure for organising and holding a demonstration.

The Galytskyy District Court sentenced the applicant to three days of administrative detention starting from 6 p.m. on 14 October 2010, with reference to the relevant provisions of the Code on Administrative Offences.

In his appeal of 18 October 2010, the applicant noted that under Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine a demonstration could be held subject to notifying the authorities and any restrictions on holding one could be imposed only by a court, so no permission was required.

In his appeal of 18 October 2010, the applicant noted that he had notified the Lviv City Council twice about the gathering of 12 October 2010 and that at the time it was held there had been no court decision prohibiting it.

In his appeal of 18 October 2010, the applicant argued that he had organised the gathering of 12 October 2010 lawfully and that the first-instance court's conclusion that he had 'held a meeting without permission of the City Council' had not been based on law as no such permission was required by domestic law.

In his appeal of 18 October 2010, the applicant challenged the police's conclusion that he had notified the authorities about the event of 12 October 2010 only a few hours in advance, claiming that he had already done so on 17 August 2010.

In his appeal of 18 October 2010, the applicant maintained that, in the absence of any lawful restrictions on holding a demonstration, demands by the police to stop such an event could not be considered lawful.
In his appeal of 18 October 2010, the applicant maintained that the law did not provide for liability for disobeying unlawful demands of police officers.

In his appeal of 18 October 2010, the applicant complained that the first-instance Galytskyy District Court had violated his right to defend himself by refusing to allow his lawyer to appear in the case on the ground that the applicant was a human-rights defender and therefore able to defend his rights himself.

In a supplement to his appeal dated 27 October 2010, the applicant complained that the first-instance Galytskyy District Court had refused to question the witnesses and to examine a video record of the peaceful demonstration of 12 October 2010.
On 27 October 2010 the Lviv Regional Court of Appeal rejected the applicant's appeal against the Galytskyy District Court's decision of 14 October 2010.

In reply to the applicant's arguments that there had been no corpus delicti in his actions, the Lviv Regional Court of Appeal noted in its decision of 27 October 2010 that those arguments should be disregarded because they were refuted by the body of evidence in the case, without elaborating further on that point.

In its decision of 19 April 2001, the Constitutional Court of Ukraine held that the time-limits for notification should not restrict the right of citizens under Article 39 of the Constitution of Ukraine, but should serve as a guarantee of this right and provide the relevant executive authorities or bodies of local self-government with an opportunity to take measures to ensure that citizens may freely hold meetings, rallies, marches and demonstrations and to protect public order and the rights and freedoms of others.

In its decision of 16 May 2012, the Kyiv Administrative Court of Appeal noted that the file contained no documents proving that notification about the demonstration less than 10 days in advance had not allowed the police to ensure public order during the demonstration and that the holding of such an event could create a real risk of riots or crimes or endanger the health of the population and imperil the rights and freedoms of others.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly of the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (2007), Section A, provide that legal provisions concerning advance notice should require a notice of intent rather than a request for permission.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly of the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (2007), Section A, provide that the notification process should not be onerous or bureaucratic.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly of the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (2007), Section A, provide that the period of notice should not be unnecessarily lengthy but should allow adequate time for the relevant state authorities to plan and prepare for the event and for the completion of an expeditious appeal to a tribunal or court should the legality of any restrictions imposed be challenged.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly of the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (2007), Section A, provide that if the authorities do not promptly present any objections to a notification, the organizers of a public assembly should be able to proceed with the planned activity in accordance with the terms notified and without restriction.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly of the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (2007), Section B, paragraph 92, provide that the notification process should not be onerous or bureaucratic, and that individual demonstrators should not be required to provide advance notification to the authorities of their intention to demonstrate.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly of the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (2007), Section B, paragraph 93, provide that the period of notice should not be unnecessarily lengthy (normally no more than a few days) but should allow adequate time for the relevant state authorities to plan and prepare for the event, for the regulatory body to give a prompt official response, and for the completion of an expeditious appeal to a tribunal or court.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly of the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (2007), Section B, paragraph 95, provide that legal provisions concerning advance notice should require a notice of intent rather than a request for permission, and that countries where a permit is required are encouraged to amend domestic legislation so as to require notification only.

The Guidelines on Freedom of Peaceful Assembly of the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe (2007), Section B, paragraph 96, provide that if the authorities do not respond promptly to a notification, the organizers of a public assembly may proceed with the activities according to the terms notified without restriction, and that even where authorization is required, authorization should be presumed granted if a response is not given within a reasonable time.

In its opinion adopted at its 64th plenary session, the Venice Commission stated that establishing a regime of prior notification of peaceful assemblies does not necessarily extend to an infringement of the right, and that such regimes exist in several European countries.

In its opinion adopted at its 64th plenary session, the Venice Commission stated that the need for advance notice generally arises in respect of certain meetings or assemblies, such as when a procession is planned to take place on the highway or a static assembly is planned to take place on a public square, which require the police and other authorities to enable it to occur and not to use powers they may validly have to obstruct the event.

The Venice Commission emphasised that the regime of prior notification must not be such as to frustrate the intention of the organisers to hold a peaceful demonstration, and thus indirectly restrict their rights.
